text.en: Before factories, weavers worked at home and merchants collected cloth. Then machines and steam changed work forever. We see how industries grew in Britain and in India.

Before factories, proto-industrialisation meant merchants gave raw material to peasant families who spun and wove at home, and then sold the cloth in the market.
In Britain, cotton mills of Richard Arkwright and the Spinning Jenny of James Hargreaves speeded up spinning, and James Watt improved the steam engine.
Factories grew in Manchester and other towns. Workers faced long hours, low wages and unemployment, and women and children were employed.
India's textile exports to Europe fell as Manchester cloth entered Indian markets. Weavers faced competition and the East India Company's control.
The first cotton mill in Bombay came up in 1854, and mills grew in Ahmedabad and Madras. Jute mills were set up in Bengal.
Jobbers recruited workers for factories and often controlled them, taking money from workers who wanted jobs.
Indian industrialists such as Dwarkanath Tagore and Jamsetji Tata invested in factories. Swadeshi in the 1900s pushed Indian-made goods.
Advertisements, labels and calendars helped sell goods, using pictures of gods and national leaders to appeal to the public.

problem.en: A mill employs 120 workers and the number doubles after expansion. How many workers now?

prompt.en: Describe the changes brought by industrialisation in India.

requiredIdeas.en: Mills in Bombay, Ahmedabad and Madras

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking industrialisation helped all workers equally

points.en: Jobbers and advertising were part of the new economy.
